opening.headline: When there is no standard to say what has improved, we learn the principles of establishing success criteria and composing an evaluation set.
body: Every time the prompt is changed, the impression is that "it seems better than before," and opinions differ as different people have different standards for what they feel is good. Without standards, it is impossible to distinguish between improvements and regressions, and the longer a system is used, the more changes accumulate, so impressions alone cannot be used as a basis.

In this class, we will sequentially look at the four conditions that a good success standard must have, the process of converting vague wishes into measurable sentences, and the representativeness, difficulty, and edge cases of the evaluation set. Next, we create standards through case explanations and correct the illusion of the evaluation set.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain success criteria and evaluation set composition principles
The representativeness and difficulty of the evaluation set can be distinguished.

screens.title: There is no standard to say what has improved
screens.lead: Read a meeting scene from a team improving their prompts. It is good to think about the reasons why opinions are exchanged but no conclusion can be reached.

paragraphs: A team is improving its ability to respond to customer inquiries. Every time the person in charge changes the prompt, the impressions come back and forth between “It seems better than before” and “No, it actually got more awkward.” Since everyone has different standards for what is good, opinions differ, and the meeting turns into who can speak more persuasively.

Without standards, it is impossible to distinguish between improvement and regression. In long-lived systems, changes accumulate over time, and if you rely on impressions from time to time, you won't know which changes worked and when performance deteriorated.

The same problem exists even before you make expensive choices like tuning or search enrichment. Without numbers to compare, you can't determine which route is better. This class covers the starting point for creating those numbers: success criteria and evaluation sets.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If you could change the statement that things have gotten better with just one number, which number would be the most convincing?

screens.outro: First, let's recall the judgment criteria we use now.

screens.title: Think about it: What numbers are you measuring for improvement?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so come up with it yourself first and then click on it.

items.prompt: By what numbers are you judging whether there is improvement?
items.answer: For example, numbers that directly link to the purpose of the task are good, such as response format compliance rate, user inquiry resolution rate, or risk response rate. If you don't have the numbers yet, that's okay. Learn how to make it in this class.

items.prompt: Who measured those numbers and with what inputs?
items.answer: Numbers have different meanings depending on the input used in the measurement. If you only measure the representative questions that come to mind by the person in charge, there may be a gap with actual operational input. Comparison is only possible when measurements are taken before and after the change with the same input.

items.prompt: If there are no numbers, what should we decide first?
items.answer: The first thing to decide is your definition of success. In this task, you write down what will be a success in one sentence, and proceed to turn that sentence into a measurable indicator.

screens.outro: Let’s start by looking at the conditions that must be met for success.

screens.title: Four conditions for good success criteria
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare a vague standard with a good standard. You can see how each of the four conditions differs.

states.label: vague standards
states.body:
“Good performance,” “safe output,” and “satisfactory response” are typical vague criteria. Since there is no set definition of what to look at to determine success, each person interprets it differently, and it is impossible to compare before and after changes.

These criteria do not meet any of the four conditions. It's not specific, it's not measurable, it's not achievable, and it's unclear how it connects to the app's purpose. Even topics that seem as blurry as safety can be converted into numbers, as seen in the state on the right.

states.label: good standards
states.body:
A good success criterion has four conditions:

Specific: State your goal, such as “accurate sentiment classification” instead of “good performance.” Measurable: Use quantitative indicators or qualitative measures that are applied consistently. Achievable: Set realistic goals based on previous experiments, research, and expert knowledge, but not unrealistic given current model capabilities. Relevance: Fits the app's purpose and user needs. Citation accuracy is important for medical apps, but less important for lightweight chatbots.

Safety can also be written numerically, such as “Out of 10,000 trials, less than 0.1% of responses were judged toxic by the content filter.”

screens.outro: Now that we know the conditions, let's follow the process of turning a vague wish into a standard sentence.

screens.title: The process of converting criteria into measurable statements
screens.lead: Click the next button to follow step by step the process of turning vague wishes into standard sentences and indicators.

visual.alt: An illustration of the stages leading from a vague wish to a standard sentence, indicator, and evaluation set.
labels: 2 Standard sentence: Contains only the facts of the policy document and mentions the product name in the first sentence
3 Indicators: Code Inspection Items / Evaluation Model Items
4 Evaluation set: Comparison before and after change with the same input

steps.title: 1 Write down the wind
steps.body: The starting point is a desire like “I want to improve the way I respond to customer inquiries.” The direction is correct, but it cannot be measured now, and everyone has different interpretations. The wind itself isn't bad, it's the material you'll need to split in the next step.

steps.title: 2 Change to standard sentence
steps.body: Change it to a sentence that gives the same decision to everyone, such as "The response contains only the facts in the policy document and mentions the product name in the first sentence." Now you can look at the response and tell if it met your criteria.

steps.title: 3 Attach indicators
steps.body: Items that can be checked by rules are scored by code. Checking the string to see if the product name is in the first sentence is sufficient. Items that require judgment, such as tone or realism, are given a scoring rubric and left to the evaluation model.

steps.title: 4 View multiple axes together
steps.body: Most use cases look at multiple axes simultaneously rather than just one accuracy. Accuracy, latency, cost, and safety are all included in the criteria, and if one axis improves but the other axis falls, it cannot be called an improvement.

steps.title: 5 Looking at the Cost of Failure Together
steps.body: Not all failures weigh the same. One incorrect refund is much more expensive than one awkward sentence. Therefore, the standards also determine which failures will be viewed more strictly.

screens.outro: Once you have measured the standard, you need to create an evaluation set that collects the inputs to be used for that standard.

screens.title: Representativeness, difficulty, and edge cases of the evaluation set
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Please check the principles for constructing an evaluation set.

data.text: A good evaluation set has three qualities. First, representativeness: it should reflect the distribution of inputs seen in production. Second, breadth of difficulty: collecting only easy inputs produces high but uninformative scores, while using only difficult inputs makes changes hard to detect. Third, edge case: deliberately include rare but disruptive inputs such as empty or very long inputs and ambiguous questions. Design tasks so they can be scored automatically. Prefer many automated evaluations, even with weaker signals, over a small number of elaborate evaluations. Evaluation data can come from production-log sampling, file uploads, or Synthetic data generation.

terms.tip: It refers to how much the evaluation set resembles the distribution of actual operational inputs. Low representativeness creates a gap between metrics and actual performance.
This means that it evenly covers everything from easy to difficult input. If you look at the results for each difficulty level separately, you can see where things fall apart.
Infrequent inputs such as empty input, very long input, and ambiguous questions are input that can easily break the system. You have to intentionally put it in to be sure.

The principle is that many questions that are automatically graded are better than a few assessments that are graded one by one by a person. Automate string matching, code scoring, and evaluation model scoring.
This is a method of supplementing by creating evaluation input using a model when there are insufficient operational logs. You need to check if it matches the actual distribution.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the principle, let us solve an example of changing a vague request for improvement as a standard.

screens.title: Case Study: Replacing “It Gets Better” with a Baseline Sentence
screens.lead: The instructor explains a hypothetical example of summary function improvement. Click the next button to see the process of turning a vague request into a standard.

steps.title: request
steps.body: There is a request to make the summary feature "better". As it is, we don't know what needs to be changed or whether the changes were successful.

steps.title: Step 1: Deconstruct the Good
steps.body: Break a good summary into its component parts. It was divided into whether the facts were accurate, whether all key items were included, and whether the length did not exceed the upper limit. Each component must be able to be judged independently.

steps.title: Step 2: Attach measurement method
steps.body: The code is checked for inclusion of required items and length. Realism is given a scoring rubric to the evaluation model and made a decision. The grading rubric includes empirical and specific sentences, such as "If there is a value that is not in the original text, it is inaccurate," and the results are received on a scale of 1 to 5 or accurate/inaccurate.

steps.title: Step 3: Set your goals
steps.body: Targets are set at realistic levels based on existing results, industry standards, and expert knowledge. Goals that are unrealistic compared to the current model capabilities will not be achieved no matter how much improvement is made, thus clouding the team's judgment.

steps.title: Step 4: Compare using the same evaluation set
steps.body: Based on this criterion, before and after changes are compared using the same evaluation set. Now, “improved” can be said in terms of numbers, such as “mandatory item coverage has gone up from a certain amount to a certain amount.” Unless the same evaluation set is used, values ​​before and after change cannot be compared.

screens.outro: Next, let's look at the optical illusion created by the evaluation set.

screens.title: Case commentary: The optical illusion of an evaluation set containing only easy inputs
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to see how the same model evaluates differently depending on the evaluation set. The instructor explains causes and responses.

states.label: Evaluation set with only representative questions
states.body:
Because the evaluation set is made up of representative questions raised by the person in charge, the evaluation value is high. The team is satisfied and ready to deploy. However, when sampling the operation log, there were many questions with typos or mixed intentions in one sentence.

In an unrepresentative evaluation set, there is a gap between actual performance and metrics. The fact that it has a high evaluation value is no guarantee that it will perform well in operation. This is the evaluation set illusion.

states.label: Evaluation set reflecting operational distribution
states.body:
We sampled operational logs to reflect the type ratio of actual input and compensated for edge cases such as typos and mixed intent. Then, view the results separately for each difficulty level. If you write down the values ​​for each section separately, you can see in which section it first collapses. This is because the easy sections mask the weaknesses of the difficult sections if you look at the average alone.

The evaluation set is not completed all at once. When a case of failure occurs in operation, the input is continuously added to the evaluation set to grow it. This way, you can always check to see if the same failures recur, and your evaluation set will increasingly resemble actual usage. Assessment data can be gathered by sampling operational logs, uploading files, or generating synthetic data. When using synthetic data, make sure the distribution is similar to the actual input.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Key theorems and connections
screens.lead: We summarize the key points of the success criteria and evaluation set. Read it and apply it to my work.

paragraphs: Success criteria should be specific, measurable, achievable, and related to the app's purpose. Vague wishes are replaced with standard sentences and indicators, and multiple axes and failure costs are looked at together.

The evaluation set mimics the operational input, has a range of difficulty levels, and contains edge cases. A large number of questions that are automatically graded are better than a small number of questions that are graded by humans, and failure cases are continuously added to increase the number of questions.
Whichever path you choose, whether tuning or prompt improvement, you can't prove improvement without a baseline.

Going back to the question in this class, the first step is to change the impression of “improvement” into a number that says “the percentage of meeting the standard sentences has increased.” For the numbers to be reliable, the evaluation set must resemble the operational input, and the same evaluation set must be used before and after the change. No matter which improvement path you choose from now on, these two will be the basis for comparison.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Choose the fastest, most reliable, and scalable scoring method among code-based, human, and evaluation models.

checks.explain: Success criteria should be specific, measurable, realistically achievable, and related to the app's purpose.
checks.correctFeedback: You have correctly matched all four conditions and examples.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some conditions and examples have changed. Think about what each condition requires in one line and pair them again.

checks.intro: Consider the evaluation set example. Just choose the one response that suits you best.
checks.q: The evaluation value was high because the evaluation set was centered on representative questions that came to mind by the person in charge. However, looking at the operation log, there were many questions with typos or mixed intentions. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Since the evaluation value is high, leave it as is and distribute it.
We sample operational logs to supplement edge cases and view them separately by difficulty level.
Reduce the number of questions in the evaluation set and replace them with a small number of sophisticated evaluations.
The evaluation set is fixed as a complete version and failure cases are not added.
checks.explain: If the evaluation set is not representative, there will be a gap between the actual performance and the metrics. It is correct to model operational inputs, supplement edge cases, and continue to grow by adding failure cases.

wrong.0: The high value of the evaluation set containing only easy inputs may be an optical illusion.
wrong.2: I think automated majority evaluation is better than sophisticated minority evaluation.
wrong.3: The evaluation set is not completed all at once, but continues to grow by adding failure cases.

checks.correctFeedback: Good. The right direction is to reinforce the evaluation set by reflecting the operational distribution.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Consider again that high values do not necessarily mean good performance. The key is whether the evaluation set resembles the operational input.

glossary.def: These are specific, measurable goals that determine the success or failure of a task.
It is a collection of inputs collected to measure under the same conditions before and after a change.
It refers to how much the evaluation set resembles the distribution of actual operational inputs.
Although rare, these are extreme or exceptional inputs that can easily break the system.
This is a table with the grading criteria broken down by item. Provide clear criteria when leaving judgment to the evaluation model.

misconceptions.myth: The only criterion for success is accuracy.
misconceptions.fact: Most use cases look at multiple axes simultaneously: accuracy, latency, cost, and safety.

misconceptions.myth: The smaller the evaluation set, the more precise it is.
misconceptions.fact: Even if the signal is somewhat weak, more automatically scored items are better than fewer items scored by humans.

misconceptions.myth: A few representative questions are sufficient for an evaluation set.
misconceptions.fact: Optical illusions are reduced when operational distribution and edge cases are reflected.

closing.lead: The key points of this class are summarized as follows.
points: Success criteria must be specific and measurable.
Replace vague wishes with standard sentences and indicators.
The evaluation set consists of representativeness and edge cases.
There is no improvement without standards.
